imo-isl-2014-a2.title: Track the distance between the two sequences
imo-isl-2014-a2.body:
Split $(0,1)$ into $I_1=(0,\tfrac12)$ and $I_2=[\tfrac12,1)$. For $x\in I_1$ we have $f(x)-x=\tfrac12>0$, and for $x\in I_2$ we have $f(x)-x=x^2-x=x(x-1)<0$. Hence
$$(a_n-a_{n-1})(b_n-b_{n-1})=\big(f(a_{n-1})-a_{n-1}\big)\big(f(b_{n-1})-b_{n-1}\big)<0$$
holds **if and only if $a_{n-1}$ and $b_{n-1}$ lie in different intervals**. So assume, for contradiction, that for every $k\ge0$ the numbers $a_k,b_k$ lie in the same interval, and let $d_k=|a_k-b_k|$; note $d_0=b-a>0$.

- If $a_k,b_k\in I_1$, then $d_{k+1}=\big|(a_k+\tfrac12)-(b_k+\tfrac12)\big|=d_k$. Moreover $a_{k+1},b_{k+1}\ge\tfrac12$, so both lie in $I_2$.
- If $a_k,b_k\in I_2$, then $\min(a_k,b_k)\ge\tfrac12$ and $\max(a_k,b_k)=\min(a_k,b_k)+d_k\ge\tfrac12+d_k$, so
$$d_{k+1}=|a_k^2-b_k^2|=d_k\,(a_k+b_k)\ge d_k\big(\tfrac12+\tfrac12+d_k\big)=d_k(1+d_k)\ge d_k .$$

So $(d_k)$ is non-decreasing; in particular $d_k\ge d_0$ for all $k$. Now we show $d_{k+2}\ge d_k(1+d_0)$ for every $k$:

- if $a_k,b_k\in I_2$: $d_{k+2}\ge d_{k+1}\ge d_k(1+d_k)\ge d_k(1+d_0)$;
- if $a_k,b_k\in I_1$: then $a_{k+1},b_{k+1}\in I_2$, so $d_{k+2}\ge d_{k+1}(1+d_{k+1})\ge d_k(1+d_0)$ (using $d_{k+1}=d_k$ and $d_{k+1}\ge d_0$).

By induction, $d_{2m}\ge d_0(1+d_0)^m$ for all $m$. The right-hand side tends to infinity, so for large $m$ it exceeds $1$. But $a_{2m},b_{2m}\in(0,1)$ gives $d_{2m}<1$, a contradiction.

Hence for some $k\ge0$ the numbers $a_k$ and $b_k$ lie in different intervals, and $n=k+1$ satisfies $(a_n-a_{n-1})(b_n-b_{n-1})<0$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-a3.title: Example, then the bounds $D\ge S$, $D\ge M/2$, $G\le\max(M,S)$
imo-isl-2014-a3.body:
**An example with $G=2D$.** Take the numbers $1,-1,2,-2$. Dave can use the order $1,-2,2,-1$ with partial sums $1,-1,1,0$, so $D\le1$. George may first pick $1$ (a tie with $-1$), then $-1$ (making the sum $0$), then $2$ (a tie with $-2$), then $-2$; the partial sums are $1,0,2,0$, so $G=2$. Also $D\ge1$ (see (2) below), so $D=1$ and $G=2D$. Hence $c\ge2$.

**Proof that $G\le 2D$ always.** Let the numbers be $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and put
$$M=\max_i|x_i|,\qquad S=|x_1+\cdots+x_n|.$$
We show
$$\text{(1) } D\ge S,\qquad \text{(2) } D\ge \tfrac M2,\qquad \text{(3) } G\le \max\{M,S\}.$$
Then $G\le\max\{M,S\}\le\max\{2D,D\}=2D$.

*(1)* The last partial sum of any arrangement is the total sum, whose absolute value is $S$.

*(2)* Let $d_1,\dots,d_n$ be Dave's arrangement and let $|d_i|=M$. Then
$$M=|(d_1+\cdots+d_i)-(d_1+\cdots+d_{i-1})|\le|d_1+\cdots+d_i|+|d_1+\cdots+d_{i-1}|\le 2D.$$

*(3)* Let $g_1,\dots,g_n$ be George's sequence, $h_i=g_1+\cdots+g_i$, $h_0=0$, and $N=\max\{M,S\}$. We prove $|h_i|\le N$ by induction on $i$. For $i=1$: $|h_1|=|g_1|\le M\le N$. Suppose $|h_{i-1}|\le N$ for some $i\ge 2$.

- *Case 1: no two of $g_i,\dots,g_n$ have opposite signs.* Say all are $\ge0$ (the other case is symmetric). Then $h_{i-1}\le h_i\le\cdots\le h_n$, so $h_i$ lies between $h_{i-1}$ and $h_n$ and $|h_i|\le\max\{|h_{i-1}|,|h_n|\}\le\max\{N,S\}=N$.
- *Case 2: among $g_i,\dots,g_n$ there are a positive and a negative number.* Then one of them, $g_j$ ($j\ge i$), satisfies $h_{i-1}g_j\le0$. Since $h_{i-1}$ and $g_j$ do not have the same strict sign, $|h_{i-1}+g_j|\le\max\{|h_{i-1}|,|g_j|\}\le N$. In step $i$, $g_j$ was still available and George minimised $|h_{i-1}+x|$, so $|h_i|\le|h_{i-1}+g_j|\le N$.

This proves (3) for every sequence George might obtain, hence $G\le 2D$, and the least constant is $c=2$.

**Answer: $c=2$.**

imo-isl-2014-a4.title: Periods of $f$ and the relation at $3m$
imo-isl-2014-a4.body:
Write $C=1007$, so $2014=2C$, and let $D=f(0)$. The equation is
$$f\big(f(m)+n\big)=f(n)+\big(f(3m)-f(m)+2C\big)\qquad(1)$$

**Step 1: $f(n+D)=f(n)+2C$ and $f(n+2C)=f(n)+4C$.** Putting $m=0$ in (1) gives $f(n+D)=f(n)+2C$ for all $n$. By induction in both directions, $f(n+tD)=f(n)+2Ct$ for all $t\in\mathbb Z$; in particular $f(D)=D+2C$, $f(3D)=D+6C$. (Also $D\ne0$, otherwise $0=2C$.) Now put $m=D$, $n=r-D$ in (1):
$$f(r+2C)=f(r-D)+f(3D)-f(D)+2C=\big(f(r)-2C\big)+4C+2C=f(r)+4C .$$
By induction, $f(n+2Ct)=f(n)+4Ct$ for all $n,t\in\mathbb Z$. $\quad(2)$

**Step 2 (claim): if $f(n+a)=f(n)+b$ for all $n$, then $b=2a$.** By induction, $f(n+ta)=f(n)+tb$ for all $t$. Taking $n=0,t=2C$ here and $n=0,t=a$ in (2):
$$f(2aC)-f(0)=2Cb\quad\text{and}\quad f(2aC)-f(0)=4Ca .$$
As $C\ne0$, $b=2a$.

**Step 3: consequences.** By (1), for each fixed $m$ the shift $a=f(m)$ changes $f$ by $b=f(3m)-f(m)+2C$. By the claim, $b=2f(m)$, i.e.
$$f\big(n+f(m)\big)=f(n)+2f(m)\qquad\text{and}\qquad f(3m)=3f(m)-2C\qquad(3)$$
for all $m,n$. The second relation says $f(3m)-C=3\big(f(m)-C\big)$, so by induction
$$f(3^km)-C=3^k\big(f(m)-C\big)\qquad(k\ge0).\qquad(4)$$

**Step 4: $f$ is linear.** Some value $d=f(a)$ is not divisible by $3$: otherwise reducing the original equation mod $3$ gives $0\equiv2014\equiv1\pmod 3$. By the first part of (3) and induction, $f(n+td)=f(n)+2td$ for all $n,t$. Since $\gcd(3,d)=1$ (and $d\neq 0$), there is $k\ge1$ with $d\mid 3^k-1$ (e.g. $k=\varphi(|d|)$ by Euler's theorem). Then $(3^k-1)m$ is a multiple of $d$, so
$$f(3^km)=f\big(m+(3^k-1)m\big)=f(m)+2(3^k-1)m .$$
Comparing with (4): $3^kf(m)-3^kC+C=f(m)+2(3^k-1)m$, i.e. $(3^k-1)f(m)=(3^k-1)(2m+C)$. Hence $f(m)=2m+C=2m+1007$ for every $m$.

**Check.** For $f(n)=2n+C$: the left side is $2(2m+C+n)+C+2m+C=6m+2n+4C$, and the right side is $2n+C+6m+C+2C=6m+2n+4C$. ✓

**Answer: $f(n)=2n+1007$.** ∎

imo-isl-2014-a5.title: Examples, then force $P(x)=x^2+1$ when $P(0)\ge 0$
imo-isl-2014-a5.body:
Call the property $(\ast)$.

**Part I: every value in $(-\infty,0)\cup\{1\}$ occurs.**

*Negative values.* Let $C>0$ and $P(x)=-\big(\frac{2x^2}{C}+C\big)$. For all real $x,y$,
$$|y^2-P(x)|=y^2+\frac{2x^2}{C}+C=y^2+\frac{x^2}{C}+\frac{(|x|-C)^2}{C}+2|x|\ \ge\ 2|x|,$$
with equality only if $y=0$, $x=0$ and $|x|=C$ at once, which is impossible. So $|y^2-P(x)|\le2|x|$ is always false, and by symmetry so is $|x^2-P(y)|\le2|y|$. Two always-false statements are equivalent, so $(\ast)$ holds, and $P(0)=-C$.

*The value $1$.* Let $P(x)=x^2+1$. Then
$$|y^2-x^2-1|\le2|x|\iff(y^2-x^2-1)^2-4x^2\le0\iff\big(y^2-(x+1)^2\big)\big(y^2-(x-1)^2\big)\le0 .$$
Factor $y^2-(x+1)^2=(y-x-1)(y+x+1)$ and $y^2-(x-1)^2=(y-x+1)(y+x-1)$, and regroup: $(y+x+1)(y+x-1)=(x+y)^2-1$ and $(y-x-1)(y-x+1)=(x-y)^2-1$. So the condition is $\big((x+y)^2-1\big)\big((x-y)^2-1\big)\le0$, which is symmetric in $x,y$. Hence $(\ast)$ holds.

**Part II: if $P$ satisfies $(\ast)$ and $P(0)\ge0$, then $P(x)=x^2+1$.**

*Step 1: $P$ is even.* Applying $(\ast)$ to $(x,y)$ and to $(-x,y)$:
$$|y^2-P(x)|\le2|x|\iff|x^2-P(y)|\le2|y|\iff|y^2-P(-x)|\le2|x| .$$
As $y^2$ runs over $[0,\infty)$, this says
$$[P(x)-2|x|,\,P(x)+2|x|]\cap[0,\infty)=[P(-x)-2|x|,\,P(-x)+2|x|]\cap[0,\infty).$$
If $P(x)+2|x|\ge0$, the left set is non-empty with largest element $P(x)+2|x|$. So the right set is also non-empty, its largest element is $P(-x)+2|x|$, and therefore $P(x)=P(-x)$. There are infinitely many such $x$. Write $P(x)=P(0)+xR(x)$ and choose $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ with $\varepsilon R(0)\ge0$. For small $t>0$ we have $\varepsilon R(\varepsilon t)>-2$, so at $x=\varepsilon t$ we get $P(x)+2|x|=P(0)+t\big(\varepsilon R(\varepsilon t)+2\big)>0$. So $P(x)-P(-x)$ has infinitely many roots, and $P$ is even.

*Step 2: $P(t)>0$ for all $t$.* Suppose $P(t)=0$ for some $t\ne0$. By continuity, $|P(y)|\le2|y|$ for all $y$ in an interval $I$ around $t$. With $x=0$, $(\ast)$ reads $|y^2-P(0)|\le0\iff|P(y)|\le2|y|$. The right side holds on $I$, so $y^2=P(0)$ for all $y\in I$, which is absurd. Hence $P$ has no zero $t\ne0$. If $P(0)=0$, then since $P$ is even, $P(x)=x^2Q(x)$ for a polynomial $Q$. For $x=0$ and $y\ne0$ the left statement $y^2\le0$ is false, so $|P(y)|>2|y|$, i.e. $|yQ(y)|>2$ for all $y\ne0$. This fails for small $y$. Thus $P(0)>0$. Since $P$ has no zeros and is continuous, $P>0$ everywhere.

*Step 3: $P$ is quadratic.* $P$ is not a constant $c$: for $x=\sqrt c$ the right statement $|c-c|\le2|y|$ holds for all $y$, but the left one $|y^2-c|\le2\sqrt c$ fails for large $y$. So $\deg P=n\ge1$, and $n$ is even, so $n\ge2$. Its leading coefficient $d$ is positive because $P>0$. Suppose $n\ge4$. Put $y=\sqrt{P(x)}$ into $(\ast)$. The left statement $0\le2|x|$ is true, so $|x^2-P(\sqrt{P(x)})|\le2\sqrt{P(x)}$, hence
$$P\big(\sqrt{P(x)}\big)\le x^2+2\sqrt{P(x)}\quad\text{for all }x.$$
For large $x$ we have $\frac d2x^n<P(x)<2dx^n$, and $\sqrt{P(x)}$ is large too. So
$$\tfrac d2\big(\tfrac d2\big)^{n/2}x^{n^2/2}<\tfrac d2P(x)^{n/2}<P\big(\sqrt{P(x)}\big)\le x^2+2\sqrt{2d}\,x^{n/2}\le(1+2\sqrt{2d})\,x^{n/2}$$
(using $n/2\ge2$ and $x\ge1$). Then $x^{(n^2-n)/2}$ is bounded for all large $x$, which is absurd since $n^2>n$. So $n=2$.

*Step 4: $P(x)=x^2+1$.* By Steps 1–3, $P(x)=ax^2+b$ with $a>0$, $b>0$. Take $x$ large and $y=\sqrt a\,x$. The left statement is $b\le2x$, which is true, so $|(1-a^2)x^2-b|\le2\sqrt a\,x$ for all large $x$. This forces $a=1$. Now take $x>b$ and $y=x+1$:
$$|2x+1-b|\le2x\iff 1\le b\le4x+1,\qquad |2x+1+b|\le2x+2\iff -4x-3\le b\le1 .$$
As $0<b<x$, these say "$b\ge1$" and "$b\le1$". One of them is true, so by $(\ast)$ both are, and $b=1$.

So when $P(0)\ge0$ the only possibility is $P(0)=1$. Together with Part I, the possible values of $P(0)$ are exactly the negative reals and $1$.

**Answer: $P(0)\in(-\infty,0)\cup\{1\}$.** ∎

imo-isl-2014-a6.title: Orbit of $1$, then $f(0)$, then induction on negative arguments
imo-isl-2014-a6.body:
**Verification.** If $f(m)=m+1$ then $m^2+4f(m)=(m+2)^2$, and $f(f(m))=f(m+1)=m+2$ provided $f(m+1)=m+2$. If $f(m)=1-m$ then $m^2+4f(m)=(m-2)^2$, and $f(f(m))=f(1-m)=2-m$ provided $f(1-m)=2-m$.
- $f(n)=n+1$ everywhere: clear.
- $f(n)=n+1$ for $n>-a$, $f(n)=1-n$ for $n\le-a$ ($a\ge1$): for $n>-a$, also $n+1>-a$. For $n\le-a$, we have $1-n\ge1+a>-a$, so $f(1-n)=2-n$.
- the third function: the same for $n\ne0$, and at $n=0$: $0+4\cdot0=f(0)^2=0$.

Now let $f$ be any solution and write $(1)$ for the equation.

**Step 1: $f(n)=n+1$ for $n\ge1$.** Let $a_k=f^k(1)$ (so $a_0=1$). Putting $n=a_k$ in (1) gives $a_{k+2}^2=a_k^2+4a_{k+1}$. Since $a_2^2=1+4a_1$ is odd, $a_2=2r+1$ and $a_1=r^2+r$. Then
$$a_3^2=(r^2+r)^2+8r+4 .$$
Both $a_3$ and $s=r^2+r$ are even, and $a_3^2\ne s^2$ because $8r+4\ne0$. Distinct even squares differ by at least $s^2-(s-2)^2=4s-4$ (trivially when $s=0$). So $|8r+4|\ge4(r^2+r-1)$, i.e. $4r^2\le|8r+4|-4r+4$. If $|r|\ge4$, then $4r^2\ge16|r|\ge12|r|+16>|8r+4|-4r+4$, a contradiction. Checking $|r|\le3$: $(r^2+r)^2+8r+4$ takes the values $16,-8,-4,4,16,56,172$ for $r=-3,\dots,3$. It is a square only for $r\in\{-3,0,1\}$.
- $r=-3$: $a_1=6$, $a_2=-5$. Choosing at each step the only sign that keeps the next square non-negative and square: $a_3^2=16$, $a_4^2=25+4a_3\in\{9,41\}$ forces $a_3=-4$, then $a_4=\pm3$, $a_5^2=16+4a_4$ forces $a_4=-3$, then $a_5=\pm 2$, $a_6^2=9+4a_5$ forces $a_5=-2$, then $a_6=\pm1$, $a_7^2=4+4a_6$ forces $a_6=-1$, $a_7=0$, then $a_8^2=1$, $a_9^2=4a_8$ forces $a_8=1$, $a_9=\pm2$. But $a_8=1=a_0$ gives $a_9=f(1)=a_1=6$. Contradiction.
- $r=0$: $a_1=0$, $a_2=1=a_0$, so $a_3=f(1)=0$, but $a_3^2=0+4=4$. Contradiction.
- $r=1$: $a_1=2$, $a_2=3$. We show $a_k=k+1$ for all $k$ by induction. Assume $a_{k-1}=k$ and $a_k=k+1$ ($k\ge2$). Then $a_{k+1}^2=k^2+4(k+1)=(k+2)^2$. If $a_{k+1}=-(k+2)$, then $a_{k+2}^2=(k+1)^2-4(k+2)=(k-1)^2-8$. The only squares differing by $8$ are $9$ and $1$, so $k=4$; then $a_5=-6$, $a_6^2=25-24=1$, and $a_7^2=36\pm4\in\{32,40\}$, which is not a square. So $a_{k+1}=k+2$.

Hence $a_k=k+1$ for all $k$, i.e. $f(k)=f(a_{k-1})=a_k=k+1$ for all $k\ge1$.

**Step 2: $f(0)=1$, or $f(0)=0$ and $f(n)\ne0$ for all $n\ne0$.** From $n=0$: $4f(0)=f(f(0))^2\ge0$. If $f(0)>0$, Step 1 gives $4f(0)=(f(0)+1)^2$, so $f(0)=1$. If $f(0)=0$ and $f(n)=0$ for some $n$, then $n^2=f(f(n))^2=f(0)^2=0$.

Consequently: **for every $t\ge0$, $f(t)=t+1$, unless $t=0$ and $f(0)=0$.** $\quad(2)$

**Step 3 (lemma): for every $n\ge1$, $f(-n)\in\{1-n,\,1+n\}$; moreover, if $f(-n)=1-n$, then $f(1-n)=2-n$.**

We prove the first part by strong induction on $n$.

*$n=1$.* $1+4f(-1)=f(f(-1))^2\ge0$ gives $f(-1)\ge0$. If $f(-1)=0$, then $1=f(0)^2$, so $f(0)=1$, which is allowed. If $f(-1)\ge1$, then $1+4f(-1)=(f(-1)+1)^2$ by (2), so $f(-1)=2$.

*Induction step, $n\ge2$.* Assume the claim for $1,\dots,n-1$. Then by (2): **for every $t$ with $|t|<n$, $f(t)=\pm t+1$ unless $t=0=f(0)$.**

- Suppose $f(-n)\le-n$. Then $u:=f(f(-n))$ satisfies $u^2=n^2+4f(-n)\le n^2-4n<(n-2)^2$, so $|u|\le n-3$ (and this case is impossible for $n=2$). If $u=0=f(0)$, then Step 2 gives $f(-n)=0$, which is false. So $f(u)=\pm u+1$. Applying (1) at $f(-n)$:
$$n^2\le f(-n)^2=f(u)^2-4u=(\pm u+1)^2-4u\le u^2+6|u|+1\le(n-3)^2+6(n-3)+1=n^2-8,$$
a contradiction.
- So $f(-n)>-n$. Put $v=f(-n)$. If $v\ge0$: $v=0=f(0)$ is impossible by Step 2, so $f(v)=v+1$ by (2). If $-n<v<0$: $f(v)=\pm v+1$ by the induction hypothesis. In all cases $f(v)=\pm v+1$. Then $n^2+4v=(\pm v+1)^2$ gives either $n^2=(v-1)^2$, i.e. $v=1\pm n$, or $n^2=(v-3)^2-8$. The latter forces $n=1$, which is excluded.

*Second part.* Let $f(-n)=1-n$ with $n\ge2$. Then $f(1-n)^2=f(f(-n))^2=n^2+4(1-n)=(n-2)^2$, so $f(1-n)=\pm(n-2)$. By the first part for $n-1$, $f(1-n)\in\{2-n,\,n\}$. As $n\ne\pm(n-2)$, we get $f(1-n)=2-n$. For $n=1$, this is the statement $f(-1)=0\Rightarrow f(0)=1$ shown above.

**Conclusion.** In terms of $x=-n<0$, the lemma says $f(x)\in\{x+1,\,1-x\}$, and $f(x)=x+1\Rightarrow f(x+1)=x+2$. If $f(x)=x+1$ for all $x$ we have the first solution. Otherwise let $m$ be the largest integer with $f(m)\ne m+1$; by Steps 1 and 2, $m\le0$. By the contrapositive of the second part, $f(m-1)\ne m$, so $f(m-1)=2-m$; repeating, $f(x)=1-x$ for all $x<m$, and also $f(m)=1-m$ if $m<0$.
- If $m=-a<0$: $f(x)=x+1$ for $x>-a$ and $f(x)=1-x$ for $x\le-a$ (second family).
- If $m=0$: $f(0)\ne1$, so $f(0)=0$, and $f(x)=1-x$ for $x<0$, $f(x)=x+1$ for $x>0$ (third solution).

**Answer:** the three types of functions listed above. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c1.title: Count corners and T-junctions
imo-isl-2014-c1.body:
Let the dissection consist of $k$ rectangles. Look at the points that are corners of at least one small rectangle. At such a point the angles of the small rectangles around it add up to $360^\circ$ (or $180^\circ$ on a side of $R$, $90^\circ$ at a corner of $R$). A rectangle containing the point at a corner contributes $90^\circ$. A rectangle containing it in the interior of a side contributes $180^\circ$. So every such point is of one of three kinds:

- a **corner of $R$**: it is a corner of exactly one small rectangle;
- a **T-junction**: it is a corner of exactly two small rectangles (either a point of a side of $R$, or an interior point where a third rectangle has it in the interior of one of its sides);
- a **crossing**: it is a corner of exactly four small rectangles.

(Three corners would leave $90^\circ$, which must be a fourth corner.) Let $b$ and $c$ be the numbers of T-junctions and crossings. Each small rectangle has $4$ corners, so
$$4k=4+2b+4c,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad b\le 2k-2 .$$

Now take a given point $P$. It is not interior to any small rectangle and lies inside $R$, so it lies on a side of some small rectangle, not on the boundary of $R$. Choose such a side, say horizontal, and extend it as far as possible inside the union of all the rectangle sides. The result is a maximal horizontal segment $\sigma_P$ through $P$. At each endpoint $E$ of $\sigma_P$ the segment cannot be continued, so $E$ is a T-junction and $\sigma_P$ is the "stem" of that T. (At a crossing, or at an interior point of a straight piece, the segment would continue. $E$ is not a corner of $R$, because $\sigma_P$ does not lie on the boundary of $R$.) At a T-junction exactly one of the boundary segments ends, so **every T-junction is an endpoint of at most one maximal segment**.

Different given points give different segments: two given points on one segment would lie on a common line parallel to a side of $R$. So the $n$ segments $\sigma_P$ have $2n$ distinct endpoints, all of them T-junctions:
$$b\ge 2n .$$
Combining, $2n\le b\le 2k-2$, so $k\ge n+1$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c2.title: Product of the numbers and AM–GM
imo-isl-2014-c2.body:
Let $P_k$ be the product of the $2^m$ numbers after $k$ steps; $P_0=1$. In a step, two factors $a$ and $b$ are replaced by $a+b$ and $a+b$, and the other factors stay the same. Since $(a+b)^2\ge4ab$,
$$P_{k+1}\ge4P_k,\qquad\text{so}\qquad P_k\ge4^k .$$
After $K=m2^{m-1}$ steps,
$$P_K\ge4^{m2^{m-1}}=2^{m2^m}=(2^m)^{2^m}.$$
By the AM–GM inequality applied to the $2^m$ positive numbers on the sheets, their sum is at least
$$2^m\cdot\sqrt[2^m]{P_K}\ge2^m\cdot2^m=4^m .$$
∎

*Remark.* The bound is sharp: pair up the sheets and add in each pair ($2^{m-1}$ steps), which doubles every number. After $m$ such rounds every sheet shows $2^m$ and the sum is $4^m$.

imo-isl-2014-c4.title: Weights $3^i(-3)^j$
imo-isl-2014-c4.body:
Place $P$ on a grid of unit cells, with coordinates $(i,j)$ ($i$ increasing to the right, $j$ upwards) chosen so that all cells of $P$ have $i,j\ge0$. Write the odd integer $w(i,j)=3^i(-3)^j$ in cell $(i,j)$. Let $\Sigma$ be the sum of the numbers in all cells of $P$.

Up to translation, each kind of tetromino has two orientations (a rotation by $180^\circ$ gives the same shape). Listing the cells relative to the lower-left cell $(i,j)$ of the bounding box and factoring out $w=w(i,j)$:

| piece | cells | sum |
|---|---|---|
| S, horizontal | $(i,j),(i{+}1,j),(i{+}1,j{+}1),(i{+}2,j{+}1)$ | $w(1+3-9-27)=-32w$ |
| S, vertical | $(i{+}1,j),(i{+}1,j{+}1),(i,j{+}1),(i,j{+}2)$ | $w(3-9-3+9)=0$ |
| Z, horizontal | $(i,j{+}1),(i{+}1,j{+}1),(i{+}1,j),(i{+}2,j)$ | $w(-3-9+3+9)=0$ |
| Z, vertical | $(i,j),(i,j{+}1),(i{+}1,j{+}1),(i{+}1,j{+}2)$ | $w(1-3-9+27)=16w$ |

Every S-tetromino covers a sum divisible by $32$. Since $P$ has a tiling by S-tetrominoes, $32\mid\Sigma$.

Now take any tiling of $P$ by S- and Z-tetrominoes, with $z_v$ vertical Z-pieces. Computing $\Sigma$ from this tiling, the S-pieces and the horizontal Z-pieces contribute multiples of $32$. Each vertical Z-piece contributes $16w$ with $w$ odd, i.e. $16$ times an odd number. Hence
$$0\equiv\Sigma\equiv16z_v\pmod{32},$$
so $z_v$ is even.

Rotate the whole picture by $90^\circ$. A rotation maps S-tetrominoes to S-tetrominoes and Z-tetrominoes to Z-tetrominoes (it preserves orientation), and it swaps horizontal and vertical pieces. The rotated polygon is still tileable by S-tetrominoes, so the same argument shows that the number of horizontal Z-pieces is even as well. Therefore the total number of Z-tetrominoes is even. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c5.title: Maximal blue set and counting blue points
imo-isl-2014-c5.body:
Let $L$ be the set of lines. Call a set of lines *good* if colouring exactly those lines blue leaves no region of $\mathcal F$ with a completely blue boundary; subsets of good sets are good. Choose a good set $B$ that is maximal under inclusion, let $k=|B|$, and colour the other $n-k$ lines red. Call a point **blue** if it is the intersection of two blue lines; there are $\binom k2$ blue points.

Regions are convex polygons, and a convex region has at most one side on any given line. Take a red line $\ell$. By maximality, $B\cup\{\ell\}$ is not good, so some region $A\in\mathcal F$ has all its sides on lines of $B\cup\{\ell\}$. Since $B$ is good, one side of $A$ lies on $\ell$, and it is the only side of $A$ that is not blue. $A$ has at least $3$ vertices, and at most $2$ of them lie on $\ell$. A vertex $v$ of $A$ not on $\ell$ is the meeting point of two sides of $A$, both blue, so $v$ is a blue point. **Associate** $v$ with $\ell$.

A region $A$ is used for at most one red line, because it has only one red side. Each blue point is a vertex of exactly $4$ regions (exactly two lines pass through it). Hence each blue point is associated with at most $4$ red lines, and
$$n-k\le4\binom k2=2k(k-1).$$
So $n\le2k^2-k\le2k^2$, i.e. $k\ge\sqrt{n/2}$, and since $k$ is an integer, $k\ge\lceil\sqrt{n/2}\rceil$. Colouring any $\lceil\sqrt{n/2}\rceil$ lines of $B$ blue (a subset of a good set) does the job. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c5.title: A sharper association giving $\sqrt n$ (IMO 2014 Problem 6)
imo-isl-2014-c5.body:
Keep $B$, $k$ and the red lines as in the first solution. Call a point **red** if it lies on a red line and a blue line. For a red line $\ell$ take a region $A\in\mathcal F$ whose only red side lies on $\ell$. List its vertices clockwise as $r',r,b_1,\dots,b_s$ ($s\ge1$) with $r',r\in\ell$. Then $r$ is a red point (on $\ell$ and on the blue line through $rb_1$) and $b_1$ is a blue point. **Associate** the blue point $b_1$ with $\ell$. Note that $\ell$ is the only red line through $r$.

**Claim: every blue point $b$ is associated with at most two red lines.** Suppose $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ are associated with $b$, with red points $r_1,r_2,r_3$ and regions $A_1,A_2,A_3$. The $r_i$ are distinct, since $\ell_i$ is the only red line through $r_i$. Each segment $br_i$ is a side of $A_i$, so no line crosses its interior: $r_i$ is the intersection point nearest to $b$ on one of the four blue rays from $b$. So the $r_i$ lie on three different rays. Two of these, say those of $r_2,r_3$, form one blue line $m$ through $b$, and $r_1$ lies on the other blue line $m'$. In $A_1$ the vertices $r_1,b$ are consecutive, so the other side of $A_1$ at $b$ lies on $m$ and ends at the nearest point of $m$ in that direction, i.e. at $r_2$ or $r_3$; say $r_2$. The other side of $A_1$ at the vertex $r_2$ lies on the second line through $r_2$, namely $\ell_2$, which is red and different from $\ell_1$. So $A_1$ has a red side not on $\ell_1$, contradicting the choice of $A_1$. This proves the claim.

Every red line is associated with some blue point, so
$$n-k\le2\binom k2=k(k-1),$$
hence $n\le k^2$, i.e. $k\ge\sqrt n\ge\sqrt{n/2}$. Again colour $\lceil\sqrt{n/2}\rceil$ lines of $B$ blue. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c6.title: The rules "compare the $k$-th smallest cards" and nothing else
imo-isl-2014-c6.body:
We prove that for sets of size $n$ there are exactly $n$ rules; here $n=100$. Write $X<Y$ for "$Y$ beats $X$", and list sets in increasing order, $X=\{x_1<\dots<x_n\}$.

**$n$ rules exist.** For $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ let rule $k$ say: $A$ beats $B$ iff $a_k>b_k$. Conditions 1–3 are clear (for 3: $a_k>b_k>c_k$). To see the rules are different, put
$$A_k=\{1,\dots,k\}\cup\{n+k+1,\dots,2n\},\qquad B_k=\{k+1,\dots,n+k\}.$$
Under rule $j$: if $j\le k$, then $a_j=j<k+j=b_j$ and $B_k$ wins; if $j>k$, then $a_j=n+j>k+j=b_j$ and $A_k$ wins. For $j<j'$, the pair $A_j,B_j$ is decided differently by rules $j$ and $j'$.

**No other rules.** Fix a rule satisfying 1–3. By condition 2, $A_n=\{1,\dots,n\}<B_n=\{n+1,\dots,2n\}$. Let $k$ be the **least** index with $A_k<B_k$. We show: for disjoint $X,Y$,
$$x_k<y_k\ \Longrightarrow\ X<Y .$$
Exchanging $X$ and $Y$ gives the converse, so the rule is rule $k$.

Let $x_k<y_k$ and choose real numbers not in $X\cup Y$ with
$$u_1<\dots<u_{k-1}<\min(x_1,y_1),\qquad \max(x_n,y_n)<v_{k+1}<\dots<v_n,$$
$$x_k<v_1<\dots<v_k<w_1<\dots<w_n<u_k<\dots<u_n<y_k ,$$
and let $U=\{u_i\}$, $V=\{v_i\}$, $W=\{w_i\}$. These are listed in increasing order, and $X,Y,U,V,W$ are pairwise disjoint.

- $u_i<y_i$ for all $i$ (for $i<k$: $u_i<y_1\le y_i$; for $i\ge k$: $u_i<y_k\le y_i$). So $U<Y$ by condition 2.
- $x_i<v_i$ for all $i$ (for $i\le k$: $x_i\le x_k<v_1\le v_i$; for $i>k$: $x_i\le\max(x_n,y_n)<v_i$). So $X<V$.
- In increasing order, $U\cup W$ reads $u_1,\dots,u_{k-1},w_1,\dots,w_n,u_k,\dots,u_n$, the same pattern as $A_{k-1}\cup B_{k-1}$ with $U\leftrightarrow A_{k-1}$. By minimality of $k$, $A_{k-1}$ beats $B_{k-1}$, so $W<U$ by condition 1. (If $k=1$, then $W<U$ by condition 2.)
- $V\cup W$ reads $v_1,\dots,v_k,w_1,\dots,w_n,v_{k+1},\dots,v_n$, the pattern of $A_k\cup B_k$ with $V\leftrightarrow A_k$. Since $A_k<B_k$, $V<W$.

So $X<V<W<U<Y$, and applying condition 3 three times gives $X<Y$.

Hence every admissible rule is one of the $n$ rules above, and for $n=100$ there are exactly $100$ rules.

**Answer: 100.**

imo-isl-2014-c7.title: A discrete length: count separating lines
imo-isl-2014-c7.body:
Call a line **red** if it passes through two points of $M$. Since no three points of $M$ are collinear, there are $\binom n2<\frac{n^2}2$ red lines. For points $P,Q$ let $X_{PQ}$ be the set of red lines $g$ such that $P$ and $Q$ lie **strictly on opposite sides** of $g$. Define the **value** of a segment $PQ$ as $|X_{PQ}|$, and the value of a set of segments as the sum of the values.

**(i) The initial value is less than $n^3/2$**: each of the $n$ segments has value less than $n^2/2$.

**(ii) Each move decreases the value by at least $2$.** Let $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $S$, interior to both, and be replaced by $AC$ and $BD$. As $|X\cup Y|+|X\cap Y|=|X|+|Y|$, it suffices to show
$$|X_{AC}\cup X_{BD}|+2\le|X_{AB}\cup X_{CD}|\qquad(1)$$
$$|X_{AC}\cap X_{BD}|\le|X_{AB}\cap X_{CD}|.\qquad(2)$$

*A basic observation.* Let $g$ be a line not through $A$ and $B$. If $g$ separates $A$ from $S$ or passes through $S$, then $g$ separates $A$ from $B$. Indeed, $g$ meets line $AB$ in at most one point, lying on the closed segment $AS$, so the segment $SB$ minus $S$ stays on one side, opposite to $A$. Similarly for $C,S,D$. Conversely, if $g$ separates $A$ from $S$, then $B$ is on the side of $S$.

*Proof of (1).* Let $g\in X_{AC}$, so $A$ and $C$ are strictly on opposite sides of $g$; in particular $g$ passes through neither $A$ nor $C$.
- If $S\in g$: $g$ passes through neither $A$ nor $B$ (it meets line $AB$ only at $S$), so $g\in X_{AB}$.
- If $S$ is strictly on $C$'s side: $g$ separates $A$ from $S$, so $g\in X_{AB}$.
- If $S$ is strictly on $A$'s side: $g$ separates $C$ from $S$, so $g\in X_{CD}$.

So $X_{AC}\subseteq X_{AB}\cup X_{CD}$, and likewise $X_{BD}\subseteq X_{AB}\cup X_{CD}$. Moreover, the red line $AB$ separates $C$ from $D$ (it crosses $CD$ at the interior point $S$), so $AB\in X_{CD}$. But $AB\notin X_{AC}\cup X_{BD}$, since it passes through $A$ and $B$. Similarly the line $CD$ lies in $X_{AB}$ but not in $X_{AC}\cup X_{BD}$. These are two different lines, which proves (1).

*Proof of (2).* Let $h\in X_{AC}\cap X_{BD}$; then $h$ contains none of $A,B,C,D$. If $S\in h$, then $h\in X_{AB}\cap X_{CD}$ by the observation. Otherwise, say $S$ is on $C$'s side (the other case is symmetric). Then $h$ separates $A$ from $S$, so $h\in X_{AB}$ and $B$ is on $S$'s side, i.e. on $C$'s side. As $h$ separates $B$ from $D$, $D$ is on $A$'s side, opposite to $C$, so $h\in X_{CD}$. Thus $X_{AC}\cap X_{BD}\subseteq X_{AB}\cap X_{CD}$.

Adding (1) and (2): $|X_{AC}|+|X_{BD}|+2\le|X_{AB}|+|X_{CD}|$.

**Conclusion.** Values are non-negative integers. After $t$ moves the value is at most (initial value)$-2t<\frac{n^3}{2}-2t$, so $2t<\frac{n^3}2$, i.e. $t<\frac{n^3}4$. Hence it is impossible to perform $n^3/4$ or more moves. ∎

imo-isl-2014-c8.title: Symmetric differences and a pairing strategy
imo-isl-2014-c8.body:
Identify each card with its set of digits, and define the **sum** of cards $C_1,\dots,C_k$ as $C_1\triangle\cdots\triangle C_k$ (the digits lying on an odd number of them). Call the players $F$ (first) and $S$ (second); each ends with $512$ cards.

**Who wins.** Each digit is on exactly $512$ cards, so the sum of all cards is $\varnothing$. Hence at the end the sum of $F$'s cards equals the sum of $S$'s cards; call it $C$. A player can make every digit appear an even number of times on his remaining cards iff he can throw out a card equal to the sum of his cards, i.e. iff he holds the card $C$. Exactly one player holds $C$. So **the player holding the card $C$ wins**; there are no draws.

**Lemma.** Let $B\ne\varnothing$. The cards split into $512$ pairs $\{X,X\triangle B\}$ (*partners*). If one card is chosen from each pair, the sum of the chosen cards is $\varnothing$ or $B$.

*Proof.* Fix $b\in B$, and in each pair let $X_i$ be the card not containing $b$. The $X_i$ are exactly the $512$ subsets not containing $b$; every digit $\ne b$ is in $256$ of them, so $X_1\triangle\cdots\triangle X_{512}=\varnothing$. Replacing some $X_i$ by $X_i\triangle B$ adds $B$ several times, so the sum is $\varnothing$ or $B$. $\square$

**Case 1: $F$ takes $\varnothing$ first. Then $S$ wins.** $S$ takes any card $A$. When $F$ takes his next card $B$ ($B\ne\varnothing$, $B\ne A$), $S$ takes $A\triangle B$. This card is different from $\varnothing,A,B$ and hence still available. Pair the cards with respect to $B$: now $F$ holds the pair $\{\varnothing,B\}$, $S$ holds the pair $\{A,A\triangle B\}$, and the remaining cards form complete pairs. From now on, whenever $F$ takes a card, $S$ takes its partner. At the end $S$ holds $A$, $A\triangle B$ and one card of every other pair. If $A$ were replaced by $\varnothing$, he would hold one card from each pair, with sum $\varnothing$ or $B$ by the lemma. So his actual sum is $A$ or $A\triangle B$, and he holds both cards. $S$ wins.

**Case 2: $F$ takes $A\ne\varnothing$ first. Then $F$ wins.**
- If $S$ answers with $B\ne\varnothing$, $F$ takes $A\triangle B$ (different from $\varnothing,A,B$).
- If $S$ answers with $\varnothing$, $F$ picks any card $B\notin\{\varnothing,A\}$ such that $A\triangle B$ is untaken, and takes $A\triangle B$. Any such $B$ works, since $A\triangle B\notin\{\varnothing,A\}$.

In both cases, pairing with respect to $B$, $F$ holds the pair $\{A,A\triangle B\}$, $S$ holds one card of the pair $\{\varnothing,B\}$, and the other card of that pair is untaken. Call it the *extra* card. The untaken cards are complete pairs plus one extra card. $F$ keeps this shape: if $S$ takes a card from a complete pair, $F$ takes its partner. If $S$ takes the extra card, $F$ takes an arbitrary card $Y$, and the partner of $Y$ becomes the new extra card. Since $S$ moves last, he takes the final extra card. At the end, $S$ holds both $\varnothing$ and $B$, $F$ holds both $A$ and $A\triangle B$, and every other pair is split between them. This is Case 1 with the roles exchanged, so $F$'s sum is $A$ or $A\triangle B$, which he holds, and $F$ wins.

**Answer: every first move except taking the empty card.** ∎

imo-isl-2014-c9.title: Orbits, flipping crossings, total curvature
imo-isl-2014-c9.body:
**Orbits.** At an intersection point $X$ of circles $c_1,c_2$ (a *cross*), let $v_1,v_2$ be the clockwise tangent vectors of $c_1,c_2$ at $X$. Arriving at $X$ clockwise on $c_1$ (velocity $v_1$), Turbo leaves anticlockwise on $c_2$ (velocity $-v_2$). Arriving anticlockwise on $c_1$ (velocity $-v_1$), he leaves clockwise on $c_2$ (velocity $v_2$). The arriving and leaving rules are reversible. So the four little arcs at $X$, in directions $\pm v_1,\pm v_2$, are joined in pairs: the arc behind $v_1$ (i.e. in direction $-v_1$) with the arc in direction $-v_2$, and the arc in direction $v_1$ with the arc in direction $v_2$. Around $X$ the four directions alternate between the two circles, so $v_1$ is adjacent to $v_2$ and $-v_1$ to $-v_2$. Thus Turbo's rule replaces the cross by two small **non-crossing** arcs, and the choice does not depend on the direction of travel. Doing this at every cross turns the circles into finitely many disjoint simple closed curves, the **orbits**. Turbo's path is one orbit, so the hypothesis says there is exactly **one** orbit. We prove more generally:

$(\ast)$ *For any $n$ circles, no two tangent and no three through a point, with every cross resolved in a non-crossing way, the number of orbits has the same parity as $n$.*

**Flipping a cross.** At a cross, the four ends $a,c,b,d$ (in cyclic order; $a,b$ on one circle and $c,d$ on the other) are joined inside the cross by one of the two non-crossing pairings $\{a,c\},\{b,d\}$ or $\{a,d\},\{c,b\}$. *Flipping* replaces one by the other. Outside a small disc around the cross, the orbits also join the four ends in pairs. This outside pairing cannot be $\{a,b\},\{c,d\}$: otherwise joining $a$ to $b$ and $c$ to $d$ straight through the cross would give two closed curves that are otherwise disjoint and cross each other exactly once, transversally. That is impossible by the Jordan curve theorem, since a closed curve that enters the inside of another closed curve must leave it again. So the outside pairing is one of the two non-crossing pairings. If it equals the inside pairing, two orbits pass through the cross. If it is the other one, a single orbit passes through. Flipping exchanges these situations and changes nothing else, so **every flip changes the number of orbits by exactly $1$**, and the new configuration is again non-crossing.

Two circles meet in $0$ or $2$ points, so the number of crosses is even. Flipping every cross therefore does not change the parity of the number of orbits. It suffices to prove $(\ast)$ after all crosses are flipped.

**After flipping all crosses.** Now at every cross the snail passes from one circle to the other **keeping** its rotational direction. So we may orient all orbits so that every circle arc is traversed anticlockwise. Each orbit is a simple closed curve, so its total turning (the total change of direction angle along it) is $+2\pi$ or $-2\pi$ (theorem of turning tangents). Let $P$ and $N$ be the numbers of orbits with total turning $+2\pi$ and $-2\pi$. The total turning of all orbits is $2\pi(P-N)$.

Count it another way. The circle arcs together make up all $n$ circles traversed anticlockwise, contributing $2\pi n$. At a cross with anticlockwise tangents $u_1,u_2$, one passage turns from $u_1$ to $u_2$ by some angle $\theta$, and the other turns from $u_2$ to $u_1$ by $-\theta$. So the turns at crosses cancel. Hence $2\pi(P-N)=2\pi n$, i.e. $P-N=n$, and the number of orbits $P+N\equiv P-N=n\pmod2$. This proves $(\ast)$.

Since Turbo's path covers all circles, there is exactly one orbit, so $n\equiv1\pmod 2$: $n$ is odd. ∎

imo-isl-2014-g2.title: Ceva, then two homothetic triangles
imo-isl-2014-g2.body:
Let $a=\dfrac{BK}{KC}$, $b=\dfrac{CL}{LA}$, $c=\dfrac{AM}{MB}$. By Ceva's theorem $abc=1$.

**Choosing the pair.** Not all of $a,b,c$ exceed $1$, and not all are below $1$. Going around the cycle $a\to b\to c\to a$, there is therefore a number $\ge1$ followed by a number $\le1$. Relabelling the triangle cyclically ($A\to B\to C\to A$ permutes $a,b,c$ and the three small triangles cyclically), we may assume $a\ge1\ge b$. Then
$$bc=\frac1a\le1\iff\frac{AM}{MB}\le\frac{LA}{CL},\qquad ca=\frac1b\ge1\iff\frac{BK}{KC}\ge\frac{MB}{AM}.$$

**A fact about inradii.** *If a circle of radius $\rho$ lies inside a triangle with inradius $r$, then $\rho\le r$.* Let the circle have centre $Z$. The distances from $Z$ to the sides $a',b',c'$ are at least $\rho$, so the area is $\frac12(a'd_a+b'd_b+c'd_c)\ge\rho s$, where $s$ is the semiperimeter. Since the area equals $rs$, we get $r\ge\rho$. In particular, **a triangle contained in another triangle has an inradius at most as large.**

**The triangle $ALM$.** Let the line through $M$ parallel to $BC$ meet $AC$ at $X$; then $\dfrac{AX}{XC}=\dfrac{AM}{MB}\le\dfrac{AL}{LC}$, so $X$ lies on segment $AL$ and triangle $AMX$ lies inside triangle $AML$. Hence $r(ALM)\ge r(AMX)=:r_1$.

**The triangle $BMK$.** Let the line through $M$ parallel to $AC$ meet $BC$ at $Y$; then $\dfrac{BY}{YC}=\dfrac{BM}{MA}\le\dfrac{BK}{KC}$, so $Y$ lies on segment $BK$ and triangle $BMY$ lies inside $BMK$. Hence $r(BMK)\ge r(BMY)=:r_2$.

**Computing $r_1+r_2$.** Let $r$ be the inradius of $ABC$. Since $MX\parallel BC$, the homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $\frac{AM}{AB}$ maps $ABC$ to $AMX$, so $r_1=\frac{AM}{AB}r$. Similarly $MY\parallel AC$ gives $r_2=\frac{MB}{AB}r$. Therefore
$$r(ALM)+r(BMK)\ge r_1+r_2=\frac{AM+MB}{AB}\,r=r .$$
∎

imo-isl-2014-g3.title: Three radical axes
imo-isl-2014-g3.body:
Let $K$ be the midpoint of $BM$, i.e. the centre of $\Gamma$, and let $D,E$ be the midpoints of $BC,AB$.

**Preliminaries.** $K\ne O$: otherwise $BM$ would be a diameter of $\Omega$, so the bisector of $\angle B$ would pass through $O$. That gives $\angle ABO=\angle OBC$, i.e. $90^\circ-\angle C=90^\circ-\angle A$, and $BA=BC$, which is excluded. The perpendicular bisector of $BM$ passes through $O$ and $K$, so it is the line $OK$, and $R$ is the intersection of $PQ$ with $OK$. Since $M$ is the midpoint of arc $AC$, $OM\perp AC$.

Let $N$ be the second intersection of line $OM$ with $\Gamma$. Since $BM$ is a diameter of $\Gamma$, $BN\perp OM$, so $BN\parallel AC$. **It suffices to show that $R$ lies on $BN$.**

**The circle $\omega$ with diameter $BO$.** The right angles $\angle BDO$, $\angle BEO$, $\angle BKO$, $\angle BNO$ show that $D,E,K,N$ lie on $\omega$. Since $OB=OC$ and $OA=OB$, the rays $OD$ and $OE$ are the bisectors of $\angle BOC$ and $\angle AOB$, so $Q$ lies on ray $OD$ and $P$ on ray $OE$.

**$O,K,P,Q$ are concyclic.** As $O$ lies inside the acute triangle, the ray $BO$ is inside $\angle ABC$, so $E$ (on $BA$) and $D$ (on $BC$) lie on different sides of the diameter $BO$ of $\omega$. Hence $B,E,O,D$ lie on $\omega$ in this cyclic order, and the chord $ED$ separates $B$ from $O$. The internal bisector $BK$ of the inscribed angle $EBD$ meets $\omega$ again at $K$, so $K$ is the midpoint of the arc $ED$ not containing $B$, i.e. of the arc containing $O$. The midpoint of the arc $ED$ containing $O$ lies on the **external** bisector of $\angle EOD$ (as $K\ne O$). So line $OK$ is the external bisector of $\angle POQ$.

Also $KP=KQ$ (radii of $\Gamma$), so $K$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$. If $OP=OQ$, this perpendicular bisector is the internal bisector of $\angle POQ$, which meets the external bisector only at $O$, forcing $K=O$, impossible. So $OP\ne OQ$. The external bisector at $O$ and the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$ then meet exactly at the midpoint of arc $POQ$ of the circle $\gamma=(OPQ)$. Hence $K\in\gamma$.

**Radical axes.** The circles $\omega$ and $\gamma$ meet at $O,K$; $\omega$ and $\Gamma$ meet at $B,N$; $\gamma$ and $\Gamma$ meet at $P,Q$. ($N\ne B$, as $B\notin OM$ because $BM$ is not a diameter.) So the radical axes of the pairs are $OK$, $BN$ and $PQ$. The point $R=OK\cap PQ$ has equal power with respect to $\omega$ and $\gamma$, and with respect to $\gamma$ and $\Gamma$. So it has equal power with respect to $\omega$ and $\Gamma$, i.e. it lies on $BN$. Therefore $BR$ is the line $BN$, which is parallel to $AC$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-g4.title: Radical centre and a constant ratio
imo-isl-2014-g4.body:
Let $\omega_A=(AMP)$ and $\omega_B=(BMC)$. For a circle tangent to $BC$ at $B$, every point $Z\neq B$ on it satisfies $BZ=d\sin\angle ZBC$, where $d$ is the diameter (tangent–chord angle). Let $\Theta$ be the circle tangent to $BC$ at $B$, on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, with diameter $d=\lambda\dfrac{AB}{\sin\angle ABC}$. Since a point $Z\ne B$ on $A$'s side of $BC$ lies on $\Theta$ iff $BZ=d\sin\angle ZBC$, it suffices to prove:

$$Q\text{ lies on the same side of }BC\text{ as }A,\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{QB}{\sin\angle QBC}=\lambda\frac{AB}{\sin\angle ABC}.\qquad(\ast)$$

**Case 1: $AP\parallel BC$.** The parallel chords $AP$ and $BC$ of $\Gamma$ have a common perpendicular bisector $s$; the reflection $\sigma$ in $s$ swaps $A\leftrightarrow P$ and $B\leftrightarrow C$. The centre of $\omega_A$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AP$, and the centre of $\omega_B$ on that of $BC$, so both centres lie on $s$. Hence the common chord $MQ$ of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ is perpendicular to $s$ and bisected by it, i.e. $Q=\sigma(M)$. Since $\sigma$ maps segment $CP$ onto segment $BA$, $Q$ lies on $BA$ with $BQ=\lambda\,BA$. Then $Q$ is on $A$'s side of $BC$, $\angle QBC=\angle ABC$, and $\frac{QB}{\sin\angle QBC}=\lambda\frac{AB}{\sin\angle ABC}$, so $(\ast)$ holds.

**Case 2: $AP$ meets $BC$ at $X$.** $X$ has equal power with respect to $\Gamma$ and $\omega_A$ (it is on $AP$) and with respect to $\Gamma$ and $\omega_B$ (on $BC$). So it lies on the radical axis $MQ$ of $\omega_A,\omega_B$:
$$XA\cdot XP=XB\cdot XC=XM\cdot XQ\qquad(\text{signed products}).$$
($X\ne B,C$ since $P\ne B,C$.)

*$A,Q,B,X$ are concyclic.* Apply Miquel's theorem to the triangle $XPC$ with $A$ on line $XP$, $B$ on line $XC$, $M$ on $PC$: the circles $(PAM)=\omega_A$, $(CBM)=\omega_B$ and $(XAB)$ pass through a common point. The first two meet at $M$ and $Q$, so $Q\in(XAB)$.

*Side of $Q$.* If $P$ is on the arc $BAC$, then $X$ is outside $\Gamma$ and $XM\cdot XQ=XB\cdot XC>0$, so $Q$ is on ray $XM$. $M$ lies inside segment $CP$, on $A$'s side of $BC$, so $Q$ is too. If $P$ is on arc $BC$ not containing $A$, then $X$ is inside $\Gamma$ and $XM\cdot XQ<0$. $M$ is on $P$'s side of $BC$, so $Q$ is on the opposite side, $A$'s side.

*The ratio.* From $XB\cdot XC=XM\cdot XQ$ and the common angle at $X$, triangles $XBQ$ and $XMC$ are similar, so $\dfrac{QB}{QX}=\dfrac{MC}{CX}=\lambda\dfrac{CP}{CX}$. From $XA\cdot XP=XB\cdot XC$, triangles $XCP$ and $XAB$ are similar, so $\dfrac{CP}{CX}=\dfrac{AB}{AX}$. In the circle $(AQBX)$, chords are proportional to the sines of the inscribed angles over them: $\dfrac{QX}{\sin\angle QBX}=\dfrac{AX}{\sin\angle ABX}$. Also $\sin\angle QBX=\sin\angle QBC$ and $\sin\angle ABX=\sin\angle ABC$, since $X$ is on line $BC$. Therefore
$$\frac{QB}{\sin\angle QBC}=\frac{QB}{QX}\cdot\frac{QX}{\sin\angle QBX}=\lambda\frac{AB}{AX}\cdot\frac{AX}{\sin\angle ABC}=\lambda\frac{AB}{\sin\angle ABC}.$$

So $(\ast)$ holds for every $P$, and $Q$ always lies on the fixed circle $\Theta$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-g6.title: Homothety at $A$, then the pole of $EF$
imo-isl-2014-g6.body:
Let $\omega_1$ be the circle $AEF$ and $\ell$ the perpendicular bisector of $EF$ (it contains $M$, $K$ and the centre of $\omega_1$). We assume $K\neq M$, so that $S,T$ are defined.

**Step 1: if $(E,F)$ is interesting, then $KE$ and $KF$ are tangent to $\omega_1$.**

Use coordinates with $M=(0,0)$, $E=(-d,0)$, $F=(d,0)$ ($d>0$), so $\ell$ is the $y$-axis. Write $K=(0,k)$ with $k\ne0$, and $A=(p,q)$ with $q>0$. The centre of $\omega_1$ is $(0,m)$, and $\omega_1$ has equation $x^2+y^2-2my-d^2=0$; as $A\in\omega_1$,
$$p^2+q^2-d^2=2mq.\qquad(1)$$
The perpendicular bisector of $MK$ is the line $y=k/2$, parallel to $EF$. So the homothety $h$ with centre $A$ mapping line $EF$ onto line $ST$ maps $E\mapsto S$ and $F\mapsto T$. Its ratio is $\lambda=\frac{2q-k}{2q}$, read off from the heights; $\lambda\ne0$, since otherwise $S=T=A$. Then the circle $AST$ is $h(\omega_1)$, so
$$(E,F)\text{ interesting}\iff K\in h(\omega_1)\iff K':=h^{-1}(K)\in\omega_1 .$$
Compute $K'=A+\frac1\lambda(K-A)$:
$$K'=\Big(p-\tfrac{2qp}{2q-k},\ q+\tfrac{2q(k-q)}{2q-k}\Big)=\frac{k}{2q-k}\,(-p,\,q)=\mu\,A^*,$$
where $A^*=(-p,q)$ is the reflection of $A$ in $\ell$, which lies on $\omega_1$, and $\mu=\frac k{2q-k}$. The line $MA^*$ meets $\omega_1$ at $A^*$ and at one more point. $M$ is inside $\omega_1$ with power $-d^2$, so that point is $-\frac{d^2}{p^2+q^2}A^*$. Hence $K'\in\omega_1$ iff $\mu=1$ or $\mu=-\frac{d^2}{p^2+q^2}$.

*The case $\mu=1$ is impossible in an acute triangle.* Here $k=q$, so $K=(0,q)$ and $AK\parallel EF$. Write $B=A+t(F-A)$ and $C=A+s(E-A)$ with $t,s\ge1$, since $F\in AB$ and $E\in AC$. The heights of $B$, $C$, $K$ are $q(1-t)$, $q(1-s)$, $q$, so $t\ne s$ (otherwise line $BC$ would be horizontal at height $\le0<q$), and collinearity of $B,C,K$ gives $K=B+\frac{t}{t-s}(C-B)$. The $x$-coordinate then gives $p(t-s)=2tsd$. By the symmetry $x\mapsto-x$ (swapping the roles of $B,C$) we may assume $t>s\ge1$, so $p>0$ and $t>1$. Then $A-C=s(A-E)=s(p+d,\,q)$ and
$$B-C=\big(d(t+s)+(s-t)p,\ (s-t)q\big)=\big(d(t+s-2ts),\ (s-t)q\big).$$
Since $t+s-2ts=-\big(t(s-1)+s(t-1)\big)<0$, $s-t<0$ and $p+d>0$, we get $(A-C)\cdot(B-C)<0$: the angle $ACB$ is obtuse, a contradiction.

*So $\mu=-\frac{d^2}{p^2+q^2}$*, i.e. $k(p^2+q^2-d^2)=-2qd^2$. By (1) this is $2mqk=-2qd^2$, so $m\ne0$ and $k=-d^2/m$. The tangent to $\omega_1$ at $F$ is perpendicular to $(d,-m)$. Its intersection with the $y$-axis, the point $(0,y)$ with $(0-d,\,y-0)\cdot(d,-m)=0$, is $y=-d^2/m$. So $K$ is the common point of the tangents at $E$ and $F$, i.e. $KE$ and $KF$ are tangent to $\omega_1$.

**Step 2: $\dfrac{AE}{AB}+\dfrac{AF}{AC}=2\cos A$ for every interesting pair.**

Now take $A$ as the origin, unit vectors $u$ along $AB$ and $v$ along $AC$, with $u\cdot v=\kappa=\cos A>0$. Let $E=ev$, $F=fu$, $AB=c$, $AC=b$, $K=xu+yv$. The circle $\omega_1$ through $0,E,F$ has equation $|Z|^2-2O\cdot Z=0$, where $O$ is its centre, so $O\cdot v=e/2$ and $O\cdot u=f/2$. The power of $K$ is $|K|^2-xf-ye$. Tangency at $E$ means $KE^2$ equals the power of $K$. Since $KE^2=|K|^2-2e(x\kappa+y)+e^2$, this gives
$$x(f-2e\kappa)-ey=-e^2,$$
and tangency at $F$ similarly gives $-fx+y(e-2f\kappa)=-f^2$. The determinant of this linear system is $(f-2e\kappa)(e-2f\kappa)-ef=-2\kappa(e^2+f^2-2ef\kappa)=-2\kappa\,EF^2\ne0$, and solving gives
$$x=\frac{e}{2\kappa},\qquad y=\frac{f}{2\kappa}.$$
(Check: $x(f-2e\kappa)-ey=\frac{ef}{2\kappa}-e^2-\frac{ef}{2\kappa}=-e^2$.) Finally $K$ lies on line $BC$, i.e. $\frac xc+\frac yb=1$, which gives
$$\frac{e}{c}+\frac{f}{b}=2\kappa,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\frac{AE}{AB}+\frac{AF}{AC}=2\cos A .$$

**Step 3: conclusion.** For two interesting pairs, $\frac{AE_1}{AB}+\frac{AF_1}{AC}=\frac{AE_2}{AB}+\frac{AF_2}{AC}$. Hence $\frac{|AE_1-AE_2|}{AB}=\frac{|AF_1-AF_2|}{AC}$. As $E_1,E_2$ lie on ray $AC$ and $F_1,F_2$ on ray $AB$, this is
$$\frac{E_1E_2}{AB}=\frac{F_1F_2}{AC}.$$
∎

imo-isl-2014-g7.title: Angle chase with the midpoint of $VC$
imo-isl-2014-g7.body:
Let $\alpha=\frac{\angle A}2$, $\beta=\frac{\angle B}2$, $\gamma=\frac{\angle C}2$, so $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=90^\circ$.

**Step 1: $B,Y,I,V$ are concyclic.** In the right triangle $IUC$ ($\angle UIC=90^\circ$, $\angle ICU=\gamma$) we have $\angle IUC=90^\circ-\gamma=\alpha+\beta$. $V$ lies on ray $IU$ beyond $U$. By the exterior angle at $U$ in triangle $BIU$, $\angle BIV=\angle BIU=\angle IUC-\angle IBU=\alpha$. Since $YV\parallel AI$, $\angle BYV=\angle BAI=\alpha$. Hence $\angle BIV=\angle BYV$, and $B,Y,I,V$ are concyclic.

**Step 2: if $I,X,Y$ are collinear, then $\angle YIA=90^\circ$.** Let line $XU$ meet $AB$ at $N$. The lines $AI$, $NU$, $YV$ are parallel.
- In triangle $YAI$, $NX\parallel AI$ gives $\frac{NX}{AI}=\frac{YN}{YA}$.
- The parallels $AI,NU,YV$ cut the transversals $A N Y$ and $I U V$ proportionally: $\frac{YN}{YA}=\frac{VU}{VI}$.
- In triangle $VAI$, $XU\parallel AI$ gives $\frac{VU}{VI}=\frac{XU}{AI}$.

Hence $NX=XU$. Moreover $\angle BNU=\angle BAI=\alpha=\angle BIU$, so $B,U,I,N$ are concyclic. Since $BI$ bisects $\angle NBU$, the chords $IN$ and $IU$ of this circle subtend equal angles at $B$, so $IN=IU$. In the isosceles triangle $INU$, $X$ is the midpoint of the base, so $IX\perp NU\parallel AI$. Thus $\angle YIA=\angle XIA=90^\circ$.

**Step 3: $VA=VC$ and $\alpha=\gamma+x$, where $x=\angle BAV=\angle BCV$.** In the cyclic quadrilateral $BYIV$, $\angle VBI=\angle VYI$. Since $YV\parallel AI$ and $IY\perp AI$, $\angle VYI=90^\circ$. So $BV\perp BI$: $BV$ is the external bisector of $\angle ABC$, and $V$ is the midpoint of arc $ABC$. Hence $VA=VC$ and $\angle VAC=\angle VCA$, i.e. $2\alpha-x=2\gamma+x$, so $\alpha=\gamma+x$.

**Step 4: $W$ lies on line $SI$, where $S$ is the midpoint of $VC$.** Triangle $VIC$ is right-angled at $I$, so $SI=SC=SV$ and $\angle SIC=\angle SCI=\angle ICB+\angle BCV=\gamma+x=\alpha$. Let $T$ be the second intersection of line $SI$ with $AX$ (on the other side of $I$ from $S$). Using $\angle AIC=90^\circ+\beta$,
$$\angle TIA=180^\circ-\angle AIS=180^\circ-(90^\circ+\beta)-(\gamma+x)=\alpha-x=\angle IAV=\angle TAI .$$
So $TA=TI$. In the right triangle $AIX$ (right angle at $I$ by Step 2), the point $T$ of the hypotenuse with $TA=TI$ is its midpoint. So $T=W$, and $W$ lies on line $SI$.

**Step 5: line $SI$ passes through $Z$.** We have $\angle VSI=\angle SIC+\angle SCI=2\alpha$, and $\angle BVC=180^\circ-\angle BAC=180^\circ-2\alpha$ ($ABVC$ is cyclic). So $\angle BVS+\angle VSI=180^\circ$, and $SI\parallel VB$. In triangle $CVB$ the line through the midpoint $S$ of $CV$ parallel to $VB$ passes through the midpoint $Z$ of $CB$. Hence $I$, $W$, $Z$ all lie on the line $SI$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-n1.title: Induction for large numbers, minimal counterexample mod $2^n$
imo-isl-2014-n1.body:
**Part I: every $m>(n-2)2^n+1$ is a sum of elements of $A_n$.** Induction on $n$. For $n=2$, $A_2=\{3,2\}$, and every $m\ge2$ is $2+\dots+2$ or $3+2+\dots+2$.

Let $n>2$ and $m>(n-2)2^n+1$.
- If $m$ is even: $\frac m2>(n-2)2^{n-1}+\frac12$, so $\frac m2\ge(n-2)2^{n-1}+1>(n-3)2^{n-1}+1$. By the induction hypothesis $\frac m2=\sum_i(2^{n-1}-2^{k_i})$ with $0\le k_i<n-1$. Then $m=\sum_i(2^n-2^{k_i+1})$ with $1\le k_i+1<n$.
- If $m$ is odd: $\frac{m-(2^n-1)}2>\frac{(n-2)2^n+1-2^n+1}2=(n-3)2^{n-1}+1$. This is an integer, so by the induction hypothesis it is $\sum_i(2^{n-1}-2^{k_i})$. Then $m=\sum_i(2^n-2^{k_i+1})+(2^n-2^0)$.

**Part II: $(n-2)2^n+1$ is not representable.** By Part I there are representable numbers $\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$; let $N$ be the smallest one, and fix a representation
$$N=(2^n-2^{k_1})+\cdots+(2^n-2^{k_r}),\qquad 0\le k_i<n .$$
Suppose $k_i=k_j=k$ for some $i\ne j$.
- If $k=n-1$, the two terms add up to $2^n$. Removing them leaves a representation of $N-2^n$, which is positive (since $N\not\equiv0\pmod{2^n}$, these were not the only terms) and $\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$, contradicting minimality.
- If $k<n-1$, replace the two terms by the single element $2^n-2^{k+1}\in A_n$: the total drops by $2(2^n-2^k)-(2^n-2^{k+1})=2^n$. This again represents $N-2^n>0$, a contradiction.

So the $k_i$ are distinct, and $\sum 2^{k_i}\le2^0+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1$. Reducing the representation mod $2^n$ gives $\sum2^{k_i}\equiv-N\equiv-1\pmod{2^n}$, hence $\sum2^{k_i}=2^n-1$, and every $k\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ occurs exactly once. Therefore
$$N=n2^n-(2^n-1)=(n-1)2^n+1 .$$
The number $(n-2)2^n+1$ is $\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$ and smaller than $N$, so it is not representable.

**Answer: $(n-2)2^n+1$.**

imo-isl-2014-n2.title: Reduce to a square condition
imo-isl-2014-n2.body:
**Case $x=y$.** The equation becomes $x^{2/3}=1$, so $x=y=1$.

**Case $x\ne y$.** By symmetry let $x>y$ and $n=x-y\ge1$. Then
$$7(y+n)^2-13(y+n)y+7y^2=y^2+ny+7n^2,$$
and cubing, the equation is equivalent to $y^2+ny+7n^2=(n+1)^3$, i.e.
$$y^2+ny=n^3-4n^2+3n+1 .$$
Multiply by $4$ and add $n^2$:
$$(2y+n)^2=4n^3-15n^2+12n+4=(n-2)^2(4n+1).$$
For $n=1$ the right side is $5$, not a square. For $n=2$ it is $0$, but $2y+n>0$. So $n\ge3$, and $4n+1=\left(\frac{2y+n}{n-2}\right)^2$ is the square of a rational number, hence of an integer. Being odd, $4n+1=(2m+1)^2$ for some integer $m\ge0$, i.e. $n=m^2+m$. Here $n\ge3$ forces $m\ge2$. Then
$$(2y+m^2+m)^2=\big((m^2+m-2)(2m+1)\big)^2=(2m^3+3m^2-3m-2)^2,$$
and both bases are positive, so $2y+m^2+m=2m^3+3m^2-3m-2$, giving
$$y=m^3+m^2-2m-1,\qquad x=y+m^2+m=m^3+2m^2-m-1 .$$
For $m\ge2$, $y=(m^3-1)+m(m-2)>0$.

**Conversely**, for these $x,y$ we have $n=x-y=m^2+m$ and $(2y+n)^2=(n-2)^2(4n+1)$. All the steps above are reversible, so $7x^2-13xy+7y^2=(n+1)^3$ and the equation holds. (For example $m=2$: $(x,y)=(13,7)$, $7\cdot169-13\cdot91+7\cdot49=343=7^3$ and $|x-y|+1=7$.)

**Answer:** $(1,1)$ and the pairs $\{x,y\}=\{m^3+m^2-2m-1,\,m^3+2m^2-m-1\}$, $m\ge2$.

imo-isl-2014-n4.title: Choose $k=p\cdot 2^m$
imo-isl-2014-n4.body:
**$n$ odd.** For $k=n^m$ ($m=1,2,\dots$), $a_k=n^{n^m}/n^m=n^{n^m-m}$, an odd integer.

**$n$ even**, $n=2t$. Fix $m\ge2$. Then
$$n^{2^m}-2^m=2^m\big(2^{2^m-m}t^{2^m}-1\big),$$
and since $2^m-m\ge2$, the bracket is odd and at least $3$. Let $p$ be an odd prime dividing it, and put $k=p\cdot2^m$.

- By Fermat, $2^p\equiv2\pmod p$, so $n^k=\big(n^{2^m}\big)^p\equiv(2^m)^p=(2^p)^m\equiv2^m\pmod p$.
- $2^k\mid n^k$ and $k>m$, so $2^m\mid n^k-2^m$.

As $p$ is odd, $k=p2^m$ divides $n^k-2^m$. Now $\frac{n^k}{k}=\frac{n^k-2^m}{k}+\frac1p$ with $0<\frac1p<1$, so
$$a_k=\left\lfloor\frac{n^k}{k}\right\rfloor=\frac{n^k-2^m}{p\,2^m}=\frac{n^k/2^m-1}{p}.$$
The integer $n^k/2^m$ is even (because $2^k\mid n^k$ and $k>m$), so the numerator is odd, and $a_k$ is odd.

Different $m$ give different $k$, since $2^m$ is the exact power of $2$ dividing $k$. So infinitely many $a_k$ are odd. ∎

imo-isl-2014-n5.title: Reduce modulo $p^a$ and lift the exponent
imo-isl-2014-n5.body:
**$p=2$.** Both expressions equal $x+y$, so all pairs with $x+y=2^k$ work: $(2,n,2^k-n)$, $0<n<2^k$.

**$p$ odd.** Let $x^{p-1}+y=p^a$ and $x+y^{p-1}=p^b$; since both are at least $2$, $a,b\ge1$. By symmetry assume $x\le y$. As $t\mapsto t^{p-1}-t$ is non-decreasing on positive integers, $x^{p-1}-x\le y^{p-1}-y$, so $p^a\le p^b$ and $a\le b$.

Now $p^b=y^{p-1}+x=(p^a-x^{p-1})^{p-1}+x$. Reducing mod $p^a$ and using that $p-1$ is even,
$$p^a\mid x^{(p-1)^2}+x=x\big(x^{p(p-2)}+1\big)\qquad\big((p-1)^2-1=p(p-2)\big).$$
- If $p\mid x$, the second factor is $\equiv1\pmod p$, so $p^a\mid x$. But $x\le x^{p-1}<p^a$, a contradiction.
- So $p\nmid x$ and $p^a\mid x^{p(p-2)}+1$. By Fermat, $x^{(p-1)^2}\equiv1\pmod p$, so from $p\mid x^{(p-1)^2}+x$ we get $p\mid x+1$.

**Lifting the exponent.** Let $p^r$ be the exact power of $p$ dividing $x+1$ ($r\ge1$), and let $N=p(p-2)$, an odd number with $v_p(N)=1$. Then
$$x^N+1=\big((x+1)-1\big)^N+1=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\binom Nj(x+1)^j(-1)^{N-j}.$$
The term $j=1$ is $N(x+1)$, with $p$-adic valuation exactly $r+1$. The term $j=2$ has valuation at least $1+2r\ge r+2$, because $p\mid\binom N2=N\cdot\frac{N-1}2$. Terms with $j\ge3$ have valuation at least $3r\ge r+2$. Hence the exact power of $p$ in $x^N+1$ is $p^{r+1}$, and so $a\le r+1$.

On the other hand $p^r\le x+1\le x^{p-1}+y=p^a$, so $a\ge r$. If $a=r$, then $x+1=x^{p-1}+y$ forces $x^{p-1}=x$ and $y=1$, so $x=y=1$ and $p^a=2$, impossible. Thus $a=r+1$, and
$$x=\frac{x^2+x}{x+1}\le\frac{x^{p-1}+y}{x+1}=\frac{p^a}{x+1}\le\frac{p^{r+1}}{p^r}=p$$
(using $x^2\le x^{p-1}$ and $x\le y$). Since $p\mid x+1$ and $x\le p$, we get $x=p-1$. Then $r=1$ and $a=2$, so $p^2=(p-1)^{p-1}+y$. If $p\ge5$, then $(p-1)^{p-1}\ge(p-1)^4=(p^2-2p+1)^2>(3p)^2>p^2$, which is impossible. So $p=3$, $x=2$, $y=9-4=5$. Check: $2^2+5=9$ and $2+5^2=27$. ✓

**Answer:** $(p,x,y)\in\{(3,2,5),(3,5,2)\}\cup\{(2,n,2^k-n): 0<n<2^k\}$.

imo-isl-2014-n6.title: Weighted count of empty intervals
imo-isl-2014-n6.body:
Let $A=a_1\cdots a_n$ and $p=a_1$. All intervals below have integer endpoints. Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of segments between consecutive marked points, and let $\mathcal T$ be the set of intervals $[x,y]$ with integers $x<y$, $0\le x\le A-1$, and no marked point in the open interval $(x,y)$. (Since $A$ is marked, $y\le A$ automatically.)

**Weights.** Give $Y\in\mathcal T$ the weight $w(|Y|)$, where $w(1)=1$ and $w(d)=2$ for $d\ge2$. A segment $X\in\mathcal S$ of length $L$ contains $L-d+1$ intervals of $\mathcal T$ of length $d$, and their total weight is
$$L\cdot1+2\big((L-1)+(L-2)+\dots+1\big)=L+L(L-1)=L^2 .$$
Each $Y\in\mathcal T$ lies in exactly one $X\in\mathcal S$. Hence
$$\sum_{X\in\mathcal S}|X|^2=\sum_{Y\in\mathcal T}w(|Y|).\qquad(1)$$

**Counting $\mathcal T$ by length.** Multiples of $p$ are marked, so all lengths are at most $p$. Fix $1\le d\le p$ and an integer $x\in[0,A-1]$, and let $r_i$ be the remainder of $x$ mod $a_i$. The open interval $(x,x+d)$ contains no multiple of $a_i$ iff $r_i+d\le a_i$, i.e. $r_i\in\{0,1,\dots,a_i-d\}$, which gives $a_i-d+1$ choices. By the Chinese remainder theorem, $x\in[0,A-1]$ corresponds bijectively to $(r_1,\dots,r_n)$. So the number of $Y\in\mathcal T$ of length $d$ is
$$f(d)=(a_1-d+1)(a_2-d+1)\cdots(a_n-d+1),$$
and (1) becomes
$$\sum_{X\in\mathcal S}|X|^2=\sum_{d=1}^{p}w(d)f(d)=2\sum_{d=1}^{p}f(d)-f(1).\qquad(2)$$

**Lemma.** *If $p$ is prime and $F$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree at most $p-2$, then $p\mid\sum_{x=1}^pF(x)$.*

It suffices to treat $F=x^k$, $0\le k\le p-2$, by induction on $k$. For $k=0$ the sum is $p$. For $k\ge1$, by telescoping,
$$p^{k+1}=\sum_{x=1}^p\big(x^{k+1}-(x-1)^{k+1}\big)=(k+1)\sum_{x=1}^px^k+\sum_{\ell<k}c_\ell\sum_{x=1}^px^\ell$$
with integer $c_\ell$. By the induction hypothesis the last sums are divisible by $p$, so $p\mid(k+1)\sum x^k$. As $1\le k+1\le p-1$, $p\mid\sum x^k$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** $f$ has integer coefficients and degree $n\le p-2$, so $p\mid\sum_{d=1}^pf(d)$ by the lemma. Also $f(1)=a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ is divisible by $p=a_1$. By (2), the sum of the squares of the lengths is divisible by $a_1$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-n7.title: Divisibility sequence modulo $x_m$ and $x_m^2$
imo-isl-2014-n7.body:
Let $x_0=0$ and $x_n=a_n/c$ for $n\ge1$. Dividing the recursion by $c$ gives
$$x_{n+1}=c^2(x_n^3-4x_n^2+5x_n)+1\qquad(n\ge0),\qquad(1)$$
so $x_1=1$, $x_2=2c^2+1$, all $x_n$ are positive integers, and $x_{n+1}=c^2x_n(x_n-2)^2+c^2x_n+1>x_n$: the sequence is strictly increasing. By (1), each $x_{n+1}$ is coprime to $c$. So it suffices to find, for each $n\ge2$, a prime dividing $x_n$ but none of $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$. Such a prime does not divide $c$, so it divides $a_n=cx_n$ but none of $a_k=cx_k$, $k<n$.

**Claim 1.** If $i\equiv j\pmod m$ ($i,j\ge0$, $m\ge1$), then $x_i\equiv x_j\pmod{x_m}$.
*Proof.* It suffices to show $x_{i+m}\equiv x_i\pmod{x_m}$, by induction on $i$. For $i=0$: $x_m\equiv0=x_0$. The step follows from (1), since $x_{i+m+1}$ and $x_{i+1}$ are the same polynomial in $x_{i+m}\equiv x_i$. $\square$

**Claim 2.** If $i\equiv j\pmod m$ with $i,j\ge2$, then $x_i\equiv x_j\pmod{x_m^2}$.
*Proof.* Again it suffices to show $x_{i+m}\equiv x_i\pmod{x_m^2}$ for $i\ge2$, by induction on $i$; the step is as before. Base $i=2$: let $L=5c^2$. By (1), $x_{m+1}\equiv Lx_m+1\pmod{x_m^2}$. Writing $\varepsilon=Lx_m$ (so $\varepsilon^2\equiv0$),
$$x_{m+1}^3-4x_{m+1}^2+5x_{m+1}\equiv(1+3\varepsilon)-4(1+2\varepsilon)+5(1+\varepsilon)=2\pmod{x_m^2},$$
so $x_{m+2}\equiv2c^2+1=x_2$. $\square$

**Claim 3.** $x_n>x_1x_2\cdots x_{n-2}$ for all $n\ge2$.
*Proof.* True for $n=2,3$ ($x_2>1$, $x_3>x_1=1$). For $n\ge3$: $x_n\ge x_3\ge x_2(x_2-2)^2+x_2+1\ge7$ (as $x_2\ge3$). So by (1)
$$x_{n+1}>x_n^3-4x_n^2+5x_n>7x_n^2-4x_n^2>x_n^2>x_nx_{n-1}>x_1\cdots x_{n-2}\cdot x_{n-1},$$
using the induction hypothesis in the last step. $\square$

**Main argument.** Let $n\ge2$. By Claim 3, $x_n$ does not divide $x_1\cdots x_{n-2}$. So there is a prime $p$ whose exponent in $x_n$ is larger than its exponent in $x_1\cdots x_{n-2}$; in particular $p\mid x_n$. Suppose $p$ divides some $x_k$ with $k\le n-1$, and take $k$ minimal. $x_1=1$, and $x_n\equiv1\pmod{x_{n-1}}$ by (1), so $2\le k\le n-2$. Write $n=qk+r$ with $0\le r<k$. By Claim 1, $x_n\equiv x_r\pmod{x_k}$, so $p\mid x_r$. By minimality of $k$ (and since $p\nmid x_r$ for $1\le r<k$), $r=0$, i.e. $k\mid n$. By Claim 2, $x_n\equiv x_k\pmod{x_k^2}$.

Let $p^\alpha$ ($\alpha\ge1$) be the exact power of $p$ dividing $x_k$. Then $p^{\alpha+1}\mid x_k^2$. Also $p^{\alpha+1}\mid x_n$, since the exponent of $p$ in $x_n$ exceeds its exponent in $x_1\cdots x_{n-2}$, which is at least $\alpha$. So $p^{\alpha+1}\mid x_k$, contradicting the choice of $\alpha$. Hence $p$ divides $x_n$ but none of $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$. ∎

imo-isl-2014-n8.title: Odd double factorials and rounding
imo-isl-2014-n8.body:
**Rounding.** $\lfloor x+\frac12\rfloor$ is an integer nearest to $x$, so
$$\Big\lfloor x+\tfrac12\Big\rfloor=x\pm\|x\|.\qquad(1)$$
Write $v_p(r)$ for the exponent of the prime $p$ in a rational number $r$, and $(2n-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)$.

**Lemma.** For every positive integer $n$ and odd prime $p$, $v_p\big((2n-1)!!\big)=\sum_{k\ge1}\big\lfloor\frac n{p^k}+\frac12\big\rfloor$.

*Proof.* The odd multiples of $p^k$ among $1,3,\dots,2n-1$ are the numbers $(2\ell-1)p^k$ with $0<(2\ell-1)p^k\le2n$, i.e. $1\le\ell\le\frac n{p^k}+\frac12$. There are $\big\lfloor\frac n{p^k}+\frac12\big\rfloor$ of them. Summing over $k$ counts each factor $2i-1$ exactly $v_p(2i-1)$ times. $\square$

**The number $N$.** Let
$$N=\frac{(2a+2b-1)!!}{(2a-1)!!\,(2b-1)!!}=\frac{(2a+1)(2a+3)\cdots(2a+2b-1)}{1\cdot3\cdots(2b-1)} .$$
Each factor on top exceeds the corresponding factor $2i-1$ below, so $N>1$. Hence some prime $p$ has $v_p(N)>0$, and since $N$ is a ratio of odd numbers, $p$ is odd. By the lemma,
$$0<v_p(N)=\sum_{k\ge1}d_k,\qquad d_k=\Big\lfloor\frac{a+b}{p^k}+\frac12\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac a{p^k}+\frac12\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac b{p^k}+\frac12\Big\rfloor,$$
so some $d_k\ge1$. Fix such a $k$. By (1), the terms $\frac{a+b}{p^k}-\frac a{p^k}-\frac b{p^k}$ cancel and
$$1\le d_k=\pm\Big\|\frac{a+b}{p^k}\Big\|\pm\Big\|\frac a{p^k}\Big\|\pm\Big\|\frac b{p^k}\Big\| .$$
A rational number with odd denominator is never a half-integer, so each of the three norms is less than $\frac12$. If any sign were negative, the right side would be less than $\frac12+\frac12=1$. So all signs are $+$. The right side is then less than $\frac32$, and as $d_k$ is an integer, $d_k=1$:
$$\Big\|\frac a{p^k}\Big\|+\Big\|\frac b{p^k}\Big\|+\Big\|\frac{a+b}{p^k}\Big\|=1,$$
with $p$ an odd prime and $k\ge1$. ∎
